parts.title: Part 1
parts.context: A man phones a country house hotel to enquire about holding a wedding reception.
script: Good afternoon, Elmstead Manor, Fiona speaking.
Oh, hello. I'm ringing about holding a wedding reception at the manor. My fiancée and I are getting married in September.
Congratulations! I'd be delighted to help. Let me take a few details first. Could I have your surname, please?
Lovely, Mr Harker. And have you got a date in mind?
We were hoping for Saturday 21 September, if that's possible.
Let me have a look at the diary. Oh dear, I'm afraid the 21st is already taken. There's another wedding that day. But the Saturday before is completely free.
Hmm. That's a week earlier than we planned, but it might actually suit her parents better, because they're flying back to Canada on the 20th. Yes, let's go for Saturday 14 September.
Wonderful, I'll pencil that in. Now, how many guests are you expecting?
We sent out 80 invitations, but two of my cousins have since asked if they can bring their partners, so I'd say 85 to be safe.
85, that's fine. In that case I'd suggest the Orchard Room. The Garden Room can hold up to 150 people, so with 85 it would feel rather empty, whereas the Orchard Room is ideal for between 60 and 100.
The Orchard Room sounds perfect. Is that the one with the glass doors onto the lawn?
That's the one. Guests can step straight out onto the terrace for photographs.
Now, receptions normally begin at 6 o'clock, but some couples prefer to start later if the ceremony is in the afternoon. What time is yours?
It's at 4 o'clock at St Anne's church in the village, and then we'd like some time for photographs. So perhaps 6.30 would be better.
6.30 it is. We can serve the food from 7.
Great. And what would the catering cost?
We have three options. The three-course dinner is 55 pounds per person, a buffet is 32 pounds, and our sharing platters, which are very popular, come to 42 pounds 50 per person.
Well, the three-course dinner is a bit beyond our budget, and I'm not sure a buffet is quite what we want. I think the sharing platters, then, at 42 pounds 50.
Good choice. Drinks are charged separately, of course.
That's fine. And do you need a deposit?
Normally it's 300 pounds, but for Saturdays in September it's 500, because they're our busiest dates. It secures the booking, and it's taken off your final bill.
Now, what about music? Have you thought about that?
I was hoping for a live band, actually. A friend of mine plays the saxophone in a jazz group.

That's certainly possible, but I should mention that bands have to finish by 10.30 because of our neighbours. If you book a DJ, you can carry on until 11.30, and we have our own sound system, so there's nothing extra to hire.
Oh, I'd rather keep the dancing going as late as possible. A DJ, then.
I'll make a note of that.
Is there anything we can't do with the decorations?

You're welcome to bring your own flowers, ribbons and balloons, and confetti is fine outside on the terrace. The only thing we can't allow is real candles anywhere in the building. Battery ones are perfectly all right, though.
Good to know. My fiancée has already bought some lanterns, so I'll ask her to check they're battery ones.

What I'd suggest now is that you come and see the Orchard Room before you commit to anything. I can hold the date for seven days without a deposit. I could email you a brochure, but nothing beats seeing it in person.
Would this Saturday morning be possible? I'll bring my fiancée.
Yes, 10 o'clock would be fine. If you decide to go ahead, you can pay the deposit then.
Brilliant. We'll see you on Saturday, then. Thanks very much for your help.

parts.title: Part 2
parts.context: The chairman of a local history society gives a talk at an open evening for people thinking of joining.
script: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to our open evening. My name's Graham, and I've had the pleasure of chairing the Thornley Local History Society for the past six years. I'm going to talk for a few minutes about who we are, what we do and how you can join in, and then there'll be tea and biscuits and a chance to ask questions.

First, a little history of our own. Some people assume we're older than we are, because several of our members look as though they remember the Romans, but in fact the society was founded in 1974 by a group of local teachers and a bookseller. They were worried that old photographs and papers were being thrown away whenever a house was cleared, and they wanted somewhere safe to keep them.

We meet on the second Tuesday of every month at 7.30. Until last year we used the library, but the room had become far too small, so we now meet at the Old Schoolhouse on Chapel Lane. There's a car park behind the building, and the hall has a hearing loop for anyone who needs it. Each meeting has a guest speaker, and the subjects range from Roman roads to Victorian ice cream.

Membership costs 18 pounds a year. It used to be 15, but we had to put the fee up two years ago because printing costs had risen. Students and anyone under 18 pay only 6 pounds. In return, you receive our newsletter, which is called Milestones and comes out four times a year, and you're welcome to join any of the outings we organise in the summer. Last year we visited a working windmill, a canal museum and a stately home, and we had a picnic, though it rained.

Our archive is one of the things we're proudest of. It holds several thousand photographs, maps and letters, and it's kept in the basement of the library, because it's cool and dry down there. It's open on Thursday mornings and members can come and look things up. Please don't be put off by the stairs, as there's a lift.
Now let me tell you about our current projects, because that's where most of the fun is.

Last spring we finished our survey of the town's war memorials. Volunteers visited every memorial in the district, recorded the names and photographed each one, and the results have now been printed as a booklet. Copies will be on sale at the back this evening for 5 pounds.

Our oral history project is going well, but we're short of helpers. The idea is to record older residents talking about what Thornley was like when they were growing up. We need people who are happy to sit down with someone for an hour and ask questions. You don't need any experience, because we'll train you, and we already have the equipment.

Then there are the canal photographs. We have about 400 pictures of the canal in its working days, and we've been scanning them for two years. We did apply for a lottery grant to pay for a new website, but unfortunately we didn't get it. So a member who's a web designer has offered to build the page for nothing, and the pictures should be online next month.

The school logbooks are a different story. The headteachers' logbooks from the Victorian period belong to the county council, and we've asked for permission to copy them. We're still waiting for a reply. I'm told it should come in the autumn, but I wouldn't hold my breath.

And finally, the parish records. We were due to start transcribing them this autumn, but the church roof needs urgent repairs and the records room has been closed, so that's been put off until next year.

If any of this sounds interesting, joining is easy. There are forms on the table by the door, or you can speak to Margaret, our treasurer, who's wearing the green scarf. You can pay by cheque or cash tonight, or by bank transfer later. We'd love to see you at our next meeting, and your first visit is free. Thank you very much, and now let's put the kettle on.

parts.title: Part 3
parts.context: Two students discuss the tutor's feedback on their group film project.
script: So, have you read Dr Hartley's feedback on our film yet?
I had a quick look last night. We got 68, which is better than I expected, honestly.
Me too. I thought we might get a lot less after the sound disaster in the middle.

Well, let's go through the comments properly. Her overall comment says, let me find it, yes, 'The images are striking and the camerawork is confident, but the story is hard to follow.' So basically it looks good but it doesn't make much sense.
Yeah, that's fair. I mean, it isn't that the filming was shaky, which is what I was most worried about. It's that we jumped around too much.
Right. I remember thinking at the time it was clever to start with the empty market and then cut back to the busy day. But I can see it's confusing for someone watching it for the first time.
What did she say about our choice of subject?
She liked it. She said the closing of the market is a topic that matters to the town. It was your idea, wasn't it? I thought it was because your gran used to have a stall there.

Well, she shopped there, but that's not why. I suggested it because I'd read that the council was going to demolish the market hall in the spring, and I thought nobody would be filming it. It was now or never.
Fair enough. Now, the part I don't understand is why we ran out of time for editing. We'd planned two whole weeks.
The editing suite was fully booked. Every group wanted it in the final week, and we only got three evenings. The laptop crashed once, but we didn't actually lose any files.
And we did film far more than we'd planned.
True, that didn't help, but we'd still have managed if we'd had the suite for longer.
Okay. So, next week's presentation. Dr Hartley wants ten minutes from each group, and then questions from the class.
Should we invite Mr Okafor, the café owner? It would be nice for him to see it.
He's probably too busy, and anyway, I think we should concentrate on rehearsing the questions and answers. That's where groups lose marks, because they haven't thought about what people will ask.
Good point. I was also going to make a handout, with a summary of the story.
I wouldn't bother. People would just read it instead of listening to us.
All right. And the written reflection? I can never remember the details.

It's just a personal account of what we learned. She says we don't need references, only our own experience, and she's already collected the forms about who did what. But she did stress that it has to be under 1,200 words, because last year some people lost marks for going over.
Okay, so I need to be concise, then. Now, what are we changing for the final version of the film? Let's start at the beginning.
She says the opening sequence, the shot of the empty market, should come after the first interview. It works better in the middle as a contrast, once we've seen the market full of people.
That makes sense. What about the interview with Mr Okafor? I loved it.
She did too, but it's far too long. She wants us to cut it by a couple of minutes, but not remove it.
That track by the band? We can't use it because of copyright. She suggests we swap it for something royalty-free.
Right. And I know the narration is a problem. I recorded it in my bedroom and you can hear the traffic.
Yes, it'll have to be done again, in the studio this time.
She didn't say anything bad about them, so I think we'll leave them exactly as they are.
Good. Let's book the studio tomorrow, then.

parts.title: Part 4
parts.context: A lecturer gives a talk on the psychology of colour in marketing.
script: Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture is about something you meet every time you walk into a supermarket, even if you've never noticed it: the psychology of colour in marketing. Companies spend enormous sums choosing exactly the right colour for a logo, a shop front or a pack of biscuits, and the question for today is whether that money is well spent.

Let me start with the colours themselves and what they are generally taken to mean in Western markets. Red is the most powerful. It's associated with energy, and also with danger, and it seems to create a sense of urgency. That's why you will see it on sale signs far more often than on any other kind of sign. Retailers believe it makes shoppers act on impulse, and they're not entirely wrong.

Blue, in contrast, suggests calm and reliability. It's the colour most closely linked with trust, so it dominates the branding of banks, which of course want you to hand over your savings without worrying.

Green has long been linked to nature, and more recently to health. People sometimes assume it is simply the colour of environmental campaigns, but marketers use it mostly on the packaging of organic products, to suggest that what's inside is natural and good for you.

Yellow is the colour the eye notices first, even from a long way off, which is why so many cities choose it for their taxis. However, too much yellow is tiring to look at, so brands tend to use it sparingly.

And finally black. It suggests sophistication, and you'll find it on the boxes of perfume, watches and other luxury goods. A plain black box tells you that what's inside is expensive before you've even read the label.

Now, how strong is the evidence for all this? You may have heard the claim that up to 90 per cent of our snap judgements about a product are based on colour alone. It appears in countless marketing books, but it can be traced back to a single, poorly documented source, so I'd advise you to treat it with great caution.

A more careful piece of work was carried out in 2018 by Dr Lena Moretti, who surveyed 600 shoppers in four countries. An earlier study had claimed that people form an opinion of a product in 30 seconds, but Moretti found that the figure was closer to 90 seconds. She also found that colour does matter, but what counts is not the colour itself but whether it fits the product. Nobody trusts a bright pink bank, for example, and a dull grey ice cream is hard to sell.

A second warning is that colours do not mean the same thing everywhere. In many Western countries white suggests purity, and it's the traditional colour for weddings, but in parts of East Asia it is associated with mourning, so a company that wants to enter those markets needs to take local advice before it designs its packaging.

There's also a practical issue of accessibility. Around 8 per cent of men have some difficulty telling certain colours apart, most commonly red and green. That means designers should never rely on colour alone to give an important message, such as a warning or a price reduction. Add a symbol or a word as well.

So what should a business do in practice? My advice is not to follow rules blindly. Before launching a new design, companies should test it with focus groups made up of the kind of people who will actually buy the product, and they should be ready to change their minds if the results are surprising. Colour can help to sell a product, but it will never rescue a bad one.
Next week we'll look at the same question from a different angle, and consider how shop layout and lighting influence what people buy. Please read the first two chapters of the set book before then.

passages.title: Redwater Quay Museum: visitor information
paras: Opening times. The museum is open from Tuesday to Sunday, 10.00 am to 5.00 pm, with last entry at 4.15 pm. We are closed on Mondays, except during school holidays, and on 25 and 26 December. In July and August we stay open until 7.00 pm on Thursdays.

Tickets. Adult tickets cost £12 and tickets for children aged 5 to 15 cost £6. Children under 5 enter free of charge. A family ticket, which covers two adults and up to three children, costs £30. Tickets bought online are £1 cheaper per person than those bought at the door. Entry is free for registered carers who are accompanying a disabled visitor. Every ticket is valid for 12 months from the date of your first visit, so you may return as often as you like during that time.

Getting here. The museum stands beside Redwater Quay, a ten-minute walk from Redwater railway station. Buses 14 and 22 stop outside the main entrance. We have no visitor car park, but there are two public car parks nearby: Quay Street, which is cheaper, and the Mill Road multi-storey, which is closer. Blue Badge holders may use the four spaces beside the side entrance, which must be booked in advance by telephone.

Facilities. There is a café on the ground floor and a gift shop by the exit. Lockers are available in the entrance hall and take a £1 coin, which is returned when you open the locker. Large bags and rucksacks must be left in a locker. Wheelchairs and folding stools can be borrowed free of charge from the information desk. Photography without flash is welcome in all galleries except the Textile Room, where light damages the exhibits. Dogs are not allowed, with the exception of assistance dogs.

Guided tours. A free guided tour of the museum's highlights leaves the information desk at 11.30 am and 2.30 pm every day. It lasts 45 minutes and there is no need to book. Tours of the Engine Hall, led by former engineers, run on Saturdays at noon. Places are limited to 15 and must be reserved at the information desk at least one day ahead.

passages.title: Olive & Thyme Restaurant: booking and allergy policy
paras: Booking. We recommend that you book, especially at weekends. Tables can be reserved online or by telephone up to 60 days in advance. Parties of eight or more must book by telephone and pay a deposit of £10 per person, which is deducted from the final bill. We hold your table for 15 minutes after the time you have booked; after that we may give it to other guests. If you need to cancel, please tell us at least 24 hours beforehand, otherwise your deposit cannot be refunded.

Allergies. We take allergies very seriously. Please tell us about any allergy or intolerance when you book and again when you arrive. Every dish on our menu is marked with symbols for the 14 major allergens. However, our kitchen handles nuts, gluten and shellfish, so we cannot guarantee that any dish is completely free from traces of them. If you have a severe allergy, we will ask the head chef to speak to you before you order. A folder listing the ingredients of every dish is available on request.

Children and celebrations. High chairs are available, and our children's menu is served until 6.30 pm. You are welcome to bring a celebration cake provided that you tell us beforehand. We charge £2 per head for cutting and serving a cake brought from elsewhere, but there is no charge if the cake was ordered from us. We also offer vegetarian and vegan menus.
Opening hours. Lunch is served from noon until 2.30 pm and dinner from 6.00 pm until 10.00 pm. We are closed on Mondays.

passages.title: Greenfield General Hospital: Volunteer Handbook
paras: A  Welcome. Thank you for volunteering at Greenfield General Hospital. Volunteers give a minimum of one four-hour shift each week for at least six months. We ask this because patients and staff come to rely on familiar faces, and because training new volunteers takes time and money.

B  Before you start. You will need to complete an identity check, a health questionnaire and a criminal records check. These checks can take up to four weeks, and you must not begin work until you have been cleared. Once you have been cleared, you will attend a half-day induction covering safety, confidentiality and infection control. You will be given two polo shirts and a lanyard free of charge; lost items can be replaced for £5.

C  Your role. Volunteers do not give medical or personal care, such as helping patients to wash or eat. Typical roles include guiding visitors at reception, taking the library trolley round the wards, befriending patients who have no visitors and helping in the hospital garden. If a patient asks you a medical question, refer them to the nurse in charge. Never move a patient or lift heavy items.

D  Confidentiality. You may see or overhear things about patients. Never discuss a patient anywhere outside the hospital, and this includes social media. Do not take photographs on the wards. If you are unsure whether you can share something, ask your supervisor. A serious breach of confidentiality may lead to the end of your placement.

E  Expenses and meals. We do not repay travel costs for journeys of less than five miles. For longer journeys we pay 25 pence per mile or the bus fare. Volunteers who complete a full four-hour shift receive a voucher for a free meal in the staff canteen. Claim forms must be handed in within one month.

F  If you cannot attend. Please telephone the volunteer office at least two hours before your shift. If you are repeatedly absent without notice, we may treat this as a resignation. Your supervisor will review your placement with you after three months and once a year after that.

passages.title: Lone working: guidance for staff
paras: Some staff, including community nurses, security officers and cleaners on evening shifts, work alone for part of their duties. Lone working is not forbidden, but it must be managed carefully, and every member of staff who works alone must have a risk assessment.

Every lone worker is paired with a buddy, usually a colleague on the same team. The lone worker must telephone their buddy at the start and end of each visit or task. If no call has been received within 30 minutes of the expected time, the buddy will try to call twice. If there is still no answer, the buddy informs the duty manager, who may contact the police after a further 20 minutes.

Personal alarms are issued by the security office and should be collected before the start of a shift. An alarm must be carried on the person, not in a bag. Staff should also carry a fully charged mobile phone and record where they are going in the shared calendar.

Staff must not enter a property or an area if they feel unsafe, and should leave at once if a situation becomes threatening. Any incident, however minor, must be reported within 24 hours using the online form.

passages.title: The River Aldwen: from open sewer to city treasure
paras: A  In the summer of 1961 a council surveyor lowered a bucket from Fenner Bridge into the River Aldwen and drew up a sample that he later described as closer to soup than to water. The river that flows through the heart of the city of Marlbeck had no fish, almost no plant life and, on hot days, a smell that drove shoppers away from the riverside market. Sixty years later, children paddle in the shallows at Mill Beach, kingfishers nest beneath the same bridge, and the Aldwen is held up at conferences around the world as proof that even a badly polluted urban river can recover. How did it happen?

B  The damage had been done over two centuries. As Marlbeck grew into a centre of wool dyeing and leather making, factories lined the banks and discharged their waste straight into the water: acids, dyes and animal fat. Household sewage joined the mixture as the population quadrupled. By the 1950s the river held almost no oxygen. The city responded by turning its back on the water. Warehouses were built without windows facing the river, bridges were lined with high walls, and few residents could remember ever walking along the banks.

C  The turning point came in 1971, when a government report named the Aldwen the most polluted river in the country. Three years later, Marlbeck and eleven neighbouring councils created the Aldwen Authority, a single body responsible for the whole river from source to sea. Unusually, it had its own income, raised through a small charge added to local water bills. Its first major project, a vast treatment works at Marsh End, opened in 1983 at a cost of £40 million. Within five years oxygen levels downstream had begun to rise and the first small fish were recorded.

D  Treating sewage was only half of the task. Industry was still the largest polluter, and the Authority was given powers to fine any firm that exceeded strict limits. Some companies fought the new rules in court; others, to their surprise, found that cleaner methods saved money, because recovered chemicals and fat could be reused. The old dye works closed for good in 1986. By 1990 industrial discharges had fallen by 90 per cent, although inspectors continued to find occasional illegal pipes for another decade.

E  A more stubborn problem lay underground. Marlbeck's Victorian sewers carry both household waste and rainwater in the same pipes, and in heavy storms the system overflowed straight into the river. In the 1990s this happened about sixty times a year. The solution, completed in 2009, was a four-kilometre tunnel beneath the riverbed, large enough to store storm water until the treatment works can deal with it. Overflows have since fallen to about twice a year.

F  Change was not left to officials alone. In 1995 a retired teacher, Joan Pellew, gathered a dozen neighbours to clear shopping trolleys from the water at Mill Beach, and the Friends of the Aldwen was born. The group now has more than 4,000 members, who collect litter, test the water every month and run workshops in schools. Their regular records proved invaluable: when salmon were seen in the river again in 2008, volunteers were able to show exactly when conditions had improved enough to allow them to return. Otters followed in 2016.

G  The riverside itself has been transformed. Where warehouses once stood, there are now flats, cafés and a footpath that runs for eleven kilometres through the city. Property prices near the water rose by 30 per cent in the decade after the footpath opened, and visitors now spend an estimated £15 million a year in the area. Yet not everyone has gained. Long-standing residents report that rents have climbed faster than wages, and some small workshops that survived the polluted years have been unable to afford the new rates.

H  Nobody in Marlbeck believes the work is finished. Runoff from farms upstream, carrying fertiliser and animal waste, still enters the water after rain, and the Authority has no power over land outside its boundaries. Scientists are also concerned about microplastics, which existing treatment does not remove, and climate change brings heavier storms that may overwhelm even the new tunnel. The river is still not clean enough for swimming, but the council hopes to open a designated bathing area at Mill Beach by 2030. For a river once declared biologically dead, it would be a remarkable change.
